title: One Mother Meets Another Mother
summary: Ten months after Tholomyès left her, Fantine walks out of Paris with her daughter Cosette and, passing an inn at Montfermeil, sees two happy little girls on a swing. She leaves Cosette with their mother, Madame Thénardier, paying fifty-seven francs in advance.
details: Spring 1818, Montfermeil, near Paris. Outside a cook-shop called the Sergeant of Waterloo, kept by a couple named Thénardier, two little girls sit laughing in the loop of a huge rusted chain hung under a wrecked cart, swung by their mother, who sings as she rocks them. A young woman with a heavy carpet-bag and a sleeping child in her arms stops to watch. It is Fantine, worn and poorly dressed, though still beautiful under the plain cap.

The narrator fills in the ten months since the picnic. Deserted, Fantine lost her friends Favorite, Zéphine and Dahlia along with the men; her letters to Tholomyès went unanswered. She can barely read and cannot write. Unable to find work in Paris and unwilling to be known as an unmarried mother, she decided to go back to her native Montreuil-sur-Mer, sold everything for about two hundred francs, dressed herself in linen and put every scrap of finery on her child, and set out at twenty-two with eighty francs and a small cough. Hugo dismisses Tholomyès for good: he became a rich provincial lawyer and a stern juryman.

Fantine sits down with the innkeeper's wife, who introduces herself as Madame Thénardier, and tells a half-true story of a dead husband and lost work. Her child, Cosette (really Euphrasie), wakes and is soon digging in the dirt with the other two. When Madame Thénardier says the three look like sisters, Fantine seizes her hand and asks her to keep Cosette for her. A man's voice from inside the shop drives the bargain: seven francs a month, six months paid in advance, fifteen francs more for expenses, fifty-seven francs in all, and the child's fine wardrobe handed over. Fantine pays nearly everything she has, sleeps at the inn, and leaves the next morning weeping in the street.

Once she has gone, Thénardier tells his wife the money will cover a note for a hundred and ten francs due the next day; her children, he says, made a good mousetrap. "Without suspecting it," she answers.

title: First Sketch of Two Unprepossessing Figures
summary: Hugo sketches the Thénardiers: a pair from the half-class between bourgeois and poor, with the stuff of a brute in her and of a blackguard in him. He claims to have been a sergeant at Waterloo; she lives on cheap romances, which is why their daughters are called Éponine and Azelma.
details: The narrator pauses to say who the Thénardiers are, promising to complete the portrait later. They belong to a bastard class of coarse people who have risen a little and clever people who have sunk, combining the vices of both. Small natures that turn monstrous if anything warms them; souls that walk backwards into darkness. Thénardier is a man one distrusts on sight, shadowy behind and threatening in front. He says he was a sergeant in the 1815 campaign and painted his inn sign himself to commemorate a feat of arms; the narrator pointedly reserves judgement on how much of this is true.

Madame Thénardier is twelve or fifteen years younger than her husband and just literate enough to devour the sentimental romances then setting Paris portresses aflame. That reading gave her a languishing manner over a coarse frame, a Pamela with a Megaera underneath. It also named the children: the elder is Éponine, the younger narrowly escaped Gulnare and is called Azelma. Hugo closes with a note that this anarchy of baptismal names, which gives the ploughboy an Arthur and the viscount a Jacques, is one small eddy of the Revolution's levelling.

title: The Lark
summary: The Thénardiers pawn Cosette's clothes, dress her in rags, feed her under the table with the dog and cat, and keep raising the price they charge her mother. By five she is the household drudge, beaten by Madame Thénardier and her daughters, and the village calls her the Lark.
details: The inn is failing. Fantine's fifty-seven francs pay off Thénardier's note, but the next month they pawn Cosette's wardrobe for sixty francs, and once that is spent they treat her as a charity child: cast-off rags, leftovers eaten from a wooden bowl under the table beside the dog and cat. Her mother, settled at Montreuil-sur-Mer, has a letter written every month and is always told Cosette is doing wonderfully. Before the first year is out Thénardier demands twelve francs instead of seven; later, having somehow learned that the child is illegitimate and that the mother cannot afford exposure, he raises it to fifteen with a threat to send the child back. Fantine pays each time.

Madame Thénardier adores her own daughters and so hates the stranger, who absorbs the blows that would otherwise fall on them. Éponine and Azelma copy their mother. The village thinks the Thénardiers generous for raising an abandoned child and assumes the mother has forgotten her. Before she is five Cosette is sweeping, carrying and running errands, and her mother's payments have begun to fall behind.

After three years the rosy child has become thin, pale and uneasy, with nothing left of her prettiness but her large sad eyes. Not yet six, she sweeps the street in rags before daylight in winter. The neighbourhood calls her the Lark, because she is small, trembling and awake before anyone else; only this lark never sings.

title: The History of a Progress in Black Glass Trinkets
summary: Fantine reaches Montreuil-sur-Mer in 1818 to find her native town transformed by a stranger who, arriving in December 1815 with a knapsack and a thorn stick, revolutionised the local trade in black glass trinkets. He saved two children from a fire the night he arrived, was never asked for his passport, and is known as Father Madeleine.
details: Book V opens by turning from Montfermeil to the mother. Fantine, who left her province ten years before, finds Montreuil-sur-Mer prosperous. The town's old industry, imitation jet and black glass trinkets, had always languished because the raw materials were dear. About the end of 1815 an unknown man settled there and made two small changes, gum-lac for resin and simply folded sheet-iron for soldered slides, which cut costs, raised wages, improved the goods and tripled profits at once.

Within three years the inventor was rich and had made everyone around him rich. Nothing is known of his origins; he arrived with a few hundred francs at most, in a workman's clothes and speech. The story goes that on the December evening he walked into town, knapsack on his back and thorn club in hand, the town hall caught fire and he ran into the flames to save the two children of the captain of gendarmes, so no one thought to ask for his passport. Afterwards they learned his name: Father Madeleine.

title: Madeleine
summary: Father Madeleine, a quiet man of about fifty, builds a great factory that employs anyone willing to be honest, and pours his profits into schools, hospital beds and a dispensary. He refuses the mayoralty in 1819 and the Legion of Honour, but in 1820 the town's pleading makes him accept the post of mayor.
details: Madeleine is about fifty, preoccupied and good. His factory has two large workrooms, one for men and one for women, kept strictly apart; he asks good will of the men, pure morals of the women and honesty of all, and is inflexible on that one point in a garrison town full of temptation. Anyone hungry can find work there. Slack seasons and misery vanish from the district.

He seems to care little for his own fortune. By 1820 he has six hundred and thirty thousand francs with the banker Laffitte, but has first spent over a million on the town: six hospital beds, two new schools with doubled salaries for the teachers ("the nurse and the schoolmaster" being, he says, the two chief functionaries of the state), an infant school, a fund for old workmen, a free dispensary in the new quarter that grew up around the factory.

The town's gossips explain him in turn as a fortune-hunter, an ambitious man and an adventurer. He goes to early mass every Sunday, which alarms the local deputy into a rival show of piety that happens to add six more hospital beds. In 1819 the King names him mayor on the prefect's recommendation; he refuses. The same year his process wins him the cross of the Legion of Honour; he refuses that too. Society's drawing-rooms open to the millionaire; he declines them, and is called an ignorant brute. In 1820 the King appoints him mayor again and the whole town begs him to accept. He gives in, apparently moved by an old woman who scolds him from her doorstep for shrinking from the good he could do. Father Madeleine has become Monsieur Madeleine, and Monsieur Madeleine becomes Monsieur le Maire.

title: Sums Deposited with Laffitte
summary: A portrait of the mayor's habits: solitary meals with a book, strolls with a gun he almost never fires, prodigious strength, country lore he teaches the peasants, secret gifts left in poor men's attics. Visitors find his supposedly mysterious room plainly furnished except for two silver candlesticks on the mantel.
details: Madeleine remains as simple as on his first day: grey hair, a sunburnt labourer's face, a wide-brimmed hat and a long coat buttoned to the chin. Apart from his duties he lives alone, eats with a book open before him, and his speech grows more polished year by year. He carries a gun on his walks but rarely uses it; when he does, his aim is unnervingly perfect, and he never shoots a harmless creature. Though no longer young he is thought enormously strong, lifting horses and freeing stuck wheels. He goes out with full pockets and comes home with empty ones.

He knows country secrets, how to keep weevils and scurf off wheat, how to guard a rabbit warren with the smell of a guinea-pig, and lectures some villagers on the uses of the nettle they are uprooting, ending: there are no bad plants or bad men, only bad cultivators. He seeks out funerals as other men seek christenings. He slips into poor men's attics at night, sometimes forcing the door, and leaves a gold piece behind.

Rumour makes his bedroom a hermit's cave of skulls and hourglasses. When some mocking young women ask to see the "grotto", he shows them at once: ugly mahogany, cheap wallpaper, and nothing remarkable but two antique candlesticks on the chimneypiece that appear to be silver, since they are hallmarked. Rumour also credits him with millions on instant call at Laffitte's; the truth is some six hundred and thirty or forty thousand francs.

title: M. Madeleine in Mourning
summary: Early in 1820 the papers report the death of Monseigneur Bienvenu, Bishop of Digne, blind in his last years and tended by his sister. The next day M. Madeleine appears in full mourning; asked if he was the Bishop's cousin, he says he was a servant in his family in his youth. He also stops every young Savoyard chimney-sweep who passes through, asks his name, and gives him money.
details: The newspapers announce the death of M. Myriel, Bishop of Digne, at eighty-two, in the odour of sanctity. The narrator adds a detail the papers left out: the Bishop had been blind for years and content to be so, with his sister at his side. There follows a long meditation on blindness and being loved, on hearing a sister's step and feeling a hand on your brow and knowing yourself the centre of another soul's care; from that paradise, Hugo says, Monseigneur Welcome passed to the other.

The local paper reprints the notice. The next day M. Madeleine is dressed wholly in black with crape on his hat. The town's little aristocracy concludes he must be related to the Bishop, and his standing rises at once. When a dowager asks whether he is the late Bishop's cousin, he says no; pressed about the mourning, he answers that he was a servant in the Bishop's family in his youth.

People also notice that whenever a young Savoyard boy wanders through town looking for chimneys to sweep, the mayor sends for him, asks his name, and gives him money. The little Savoyards tell one another, and a great many come that way.

title: Vague Flashes on the Horizon
summary: By 1821 the whole district venerates the mayor, except one man: Javert, a police inspector born in prison to a fortune-teller, who worships authority and despises anyone who has ever broken the law. Javert watches M. Madeleine with steady suspicion, seems to have made inquiries about him elsewhere, and once mutters "I think I have him!" before falling silent for three days.
details: Opposition to Madeleine fades into universal respect; people travel ten leagues to have him settle their disputes. One man escapes the contagion. A tall figure in an iron-grey coat with a heavy cane and battered hat turns to stare after the mayor in the street with a grimace that says: I have seen that man somewhere, and I am not his dupe. His name is Javert; he is the town's police inspector, posted there after Madeleine's fortune was already made, through the protection of M. Chabouillet, secretary to the Paris prefect of police.

Hugo describes him through his theory that every man carries an animal inside him: Javert is the dog born in a litter of wolves. Born in prison to a fortune-teller whose husband was in the galleys, he grew up feeling outside society and saw only two ways back, to attack it or to guard it. He chose the police, served in his youth as a guard in the southern convict prisons, and is an inspector at forty. His face is a flat nose, deep nostrils and huge whiskers; serious, he is a watchdog, laughing, a tiger.

He is made of two feelings pushed to excess: respect for authority and hatred of rebellion, under which he files every crime. The functionary can never be wrong; the convict can never be redeemed. He would arrest his own father and denounce his mother and feel virtuous doing it. He has no vices, reads although he hates books, and allows himself a pinch of snuff when pleased with himself. Vagrants are petrified by his name.

Javert's eye rests constantly on M. Madeleine, who notices and treats him with the same courtesy as everyone else. From words Javert lets slip it is guessed that he has quietly searched the mayor's past elsewhere and knows that someone gathered information in a certain district about a family that had disappeared. Once he says to himself, "I think I have him!" and then is silent for three days, as if the thread had broken. Madeleine's calm disconcerts him, until one day something happens.

title: Father Fauchelevent
summary: Old Fauchelevent, a ruined ex-notary who hates the mayor, is pinned under his loaded cart in the mud. With the jackscrew a quarter of an hour away and no one willing to crawl under, Javert remarks that he has known only one man strong enough, a convict at Toulon. Madeleine crawls under the cart and lifts it on his back.
details: Passing through an unpaved lane one morning, M. Madeleine finds a crowd around an accident. Father Fauchelevent's horse has fallen with two broken legs and the old man lies caught beneath his heavily laden cart, the whole weight on his chest. Fauchelevent, a former notary and near-educated peasant, had watched this simple workman grow rich while he went bankrupt, hated him for it and tried to injure him at every turn; with nothing left but a horse and cart he had become a carter. Javert, already on the scene, has sent for a jackscrew from the farrier, a quarter of an hour away.

The cart is sinking into the rain-soaked ground and will crush the old man's ribs in five minutes. Madeleine offers five louis, then ten, then twenty to anyone who will crawl under and lift it with his back. No one moves. A voice says it is not will that is lacking but strength: Javert, watching the mayor fixedly, says he has only ever known one man able to do such a thing, a convict in the galleys at Toulon. Madeleine shudders and turns pale.

Fauchelevent screams that he is strangling. Madeleine meets Javert's eye, looks at the motionless peasants, smiles sadly, and drops to his knees under the cart. Twice he fails; the crowd and Fauchelevent himself beg him to come out. Then the mass quivers and rises, twenty arms seize it, and the old man is dragged free. Madeleine stands, pale, muddy and dripping, while Fauchelevent kisses his knees and calls him the good God. His tranquil eye rests on Javert, who is still staring at him.

title: Fauchelevent Becomes a Gardener in Paris
summary: Madeleine pays Fauchelevent a thousand francs for his dead horse and broken cart and finds him a post as gardener in a convent in Paris. When Madeleine becomes mayor, Javert shudders like a watchdog smelling a wolf in his master's clothes and avoids him. Fantine returns to the town and is taken on in the factory's women's workroom.
details: Fauchelevent's kneecap is dislocated. Madeleine has him nursed in the infirmary he keeps in his factory, and the next morning the old man finds a thousand-franc note on his bedside table with the words "I purchase your horse and cart", though the horse is dead and the cart wrecked. His knee stays stiff, and on the recommendation of the sisters and the priest Madeleine gets him a place as gardener in a women's convent in the Rue Saint-Antoine in Paris.

Some time later Madeleine is made mayor. The first time Javert sees him in the mayor's scarf he feels the shudder of a watchdog that smells a wolf in its master's clothes. From then on he avoids him and, when duty forces a meeting, addresses him with profound respect. Hugo adds an invisible sign of the town's prosperity: in seven years the cost of collecting taxes in the arrondissement falls by three quarters, and the finance minister Villèle cites it as a model.

Into this town Fantine returns. No one remembers her. The door of M. Madeleine's factory is like a friend's face; she is admitted to the women's workroom, learns a trade wholly new to her, earns little, but enough. She is making her living.

title: Madame Victurnien Expends Thirty Francs on Morality
summary: Fantine's frequent letters to Montfermeil make the workroom gossip. A bigoted widow, Madame Victurnien, pays for a trip to Montfermeil, sees the child, and spreads the news. After more than a year at the factory, Fantine is handed fifty francs in the mayor's name, dismissed, and told to leave the district.
details: Earning her bread honestly, Fantine is briefly almost happy. She buys a mirror, rents a little room, furnishes it on credit, and pays the Thénardiers promptly, writing through a public letter-writer since she can only sign her name. The letters are noticed. Hugo digresses on the idle who spy on their neighbours for the pure itch of knowing, at great cost to themselves and often ruinous to others.

Fantine is watched, envied for her golden hair and white teeth, seen wiping away tears at her bench. Her letters go twice a month to a Monsieur Thénardier, innkeeper at Montfermeil; the letter-writer is made tipsy and talks; it comes out that she has a child. An old woman makes the journey and reports, for her thirty-five francs, "I have seen the child." She is Madame Victurnien, fifty-six, widow of a monk who left his cloister in a red cap in '93, soured by him and turned fierce bigot at the Restoration, in favour with the bishop's palace at Arras.

More than a year after Fantine joined the factory, the superintendent of the women's workroom hands her fifty francs from the mayor, tells her she is dismissed, and asks her, in the mayor's name, to leave the neighbourhood. It is the very month the Thénardiers raise their price from twelve to fifteen francs. In debt for rent and furniture, Fantine cannot leave. Overwhelmed with shame, she does not dare go to the mayor; he gave fifty francs because he is good and dismissed her because he is just, she thinks, and she bows to it.

title: Madame Victurnien’s Success
summary: M. Madeleine knew nothing of the dismissal: the pious superintendent judged and executed Fantine on her own authority. No one will hire Fantine as a servant, her creditors will not let her leave, and she sews soldiers' shirts for twelve sous a day. An old neighbour, Marguerite, teaches her how to live on nothing.
details: The mayor almost never enters the women's workroom and has given full authority to its superintendent, a respectable elderly spinster recommended by the priest, who has the charity that gives but not the charity that understands and forgives. She tried, condemned and dismissed Fantine convinced she was doing right, and paid the fifty francs out of a relief fund Madeleine had entrusted to her without asking for accounts.

Fantine seeks work as a servant and is refused everywhere. The second-hand dealer threatens to have her arrested as a thief if she leaves; her landlord tells her she is young and pretty and can pay. She divides the fifty francs between them, gives back most of the furniture, and is left with a bed, no trade and fifty francs of debt. She sews coarse shirts for the garrison at twelve sous a day while her child costs ten, and begins to pay the Thénardiers irregularly.

Her neighbour Marguerite, a pious old spinster who lights her candle for her at night, teaches her the art of poverty: no fire in winter, a petticoat made from a coverlet and a coverlet from a petticoat, meals eaten by the light of the window opposite. Fantine regains a little courage and thinks of sending for Cosette, but cannot share such destitution or pay what she owes or the fare.

At first too ashamed to go out, she feels the town's scorn like a north wind when she does. After two or three months she decides it is all the same to her and walks with her head up and a bitter smile, growing brazen. Madame Victurnien watches her from her window and congratulates herself. The work wears Fantine out; her dry cough grows and her hands are hot. Only combing her beautiful hair in the morning still gives her a moment of pleasure.

title: Result of the Success
summary: Told that Cosette is naked in the cold, Fantine sells her hair for ten francs; told she is dying of a fever, she sells her two front teeth for forty. Both letters are Thénardier lies. Hating the mayor who dismissed her, hounded by creditors, earning nine sous a day, she gets a demand for a hundred francs and sells what is left: she becomes a prostitute.
details: A second winter brings short days and less work. The Thénardiers write that little Cosette is naked in the cold and needs ten francs for a woollen skirt. That evening Fantine goes to a barber, lets down hair that falls to her knees, and sells it for ten francs. She sends a knitted petticoat; the Thénardiers, who wanted money, give it to Éponine, and the Lark goes on shivering. Fantine tells herself her child is clothed in her hair.

Dark thoughts take hold. She comes to hate everyone, and most of all Father Madeleine, whom she blames for everything, and laughs and sings when she passes the factory. She takes a lover out of bravado, a beggar musician who beats her and leaves her. Her cough does not leave her. Then a letter: Cosette has a miliary fever, the drugs are ruinous, send forty francs within the week or the child dies. Fantine laughs wildly at the impossible sum, yet keeps going back to the staircase window to reread it.

In the square a travelling quack dentist offers her a gold napoleon apiece for her two front teeth. She flees in horror, then that evening is seen turning towards the inns. Next morning Marguerite finds her sitting on her bed, grown ten years older, with two napoleons glittering on the table and a black hole in her bloody smile. She sends the forty francs. Cosette was never ill; it was a trick to get money.

Fantine throws away her mirror, moves to an attic under the roof, loses her coquetry, stops mending her clothes. A prison contractor undercuts prices and her seventeen-hour days now earn nine sous. Creditors harass her on the stairs; she feels hunted and something of the wild beast grows in her. Thénardier writes that he must have a hundred francs at once or he will turn the convalescent child out into the street. She decides to sell what is left. The unfortunate girl becomes a woman of the town.

title: Christus Nos Liberavit
summary: A short chapter of commentary: Fantine's story is society buying a slave from misery. Slavery has not left Europe, Hugo says; it weighs on women and is called prostitution. Fantine has become marble by becoming mire and believes she has reached the bottom, but fate is never exhausted.
details: Hugo steps out of the story to name what has happened: society purchasing a slave from hunger, cold, isolation and destitution, a soul for a morsel of bread. Christ's law governs our civilisation but does not yet permeate it; slavery survives in Europe, falling on the woman alone, on grace, weakness, beauty and maternity, and is called prostitution.

Nothing is left of the Fantine who was. She has become marble in becoming mire; she endures, ignores, no longer avoids anything, a sponge already soaked. She believes it so. But it is an error, Hugo warns, to think fate can be exhausted or that anything has a bottom. Who knows where these driven lives are going? One alone sees the whole of the shadow, and his name is God.

title: M. Bamatabois’s Inactivity
summary: On a snowy evening around New Year 1823, a provincial dandy named Bamatabois amuses himself by taunting a toothless woman in a ball-dress outside the officers' café, then stuffs snow down her bare back. She flies at him with her nails; it is Fantine. A tall man breaks through the crowd, seizes her, and says "Follow me!" It is Javert.
details: Hugo opens with a portrait of the small-town idler: the young man with fifteen hundred francs a year who hisses actresses, quarrels with officers, smokes, yawns and never works, dressed in the triple waistcoats, codfish-tail coat, spurs and moustache of the period. Tholomyès, had he stayed in his province, would have been one of them. Hats mark politics: narrow-brimmed morillos for royalists, wide bolivars for liberals.

Eight or ten months after Fantine's fall, towards the first of January 1823, one such dandy in a morillo and a great cloak, known as M. Bamatabois, stands smoking in the snow outside the officers' café and flings an insult at a bare-shouldered woman in a ball-dress each time she passes: how ugly you are, you have no teeth. She never answers or looks at him. Piqued, he creeps up behind her and thrusts a handful of snow between her bare shoulders.

The woman roars, whirls, and hurls herself on him, clawing his face and pouring out gutter oaths in a brandy-roughened voice from a mouth missing its two front teeth. It is Fantine. Officers pour out of the café and a laughing circle forms around the struggling pair. Suddenly a tall man pushes through, grips her by her muddy satin bodice and says "Follow me!" Her fury dies; she turns pale and trembles. She has recognised Javert. Bamatabois slips away.

title: The Solution of Some Questions Connected with the Municipal Police
summary: At the station Javert sentences Fantine to six months in prison and is unmoved by her pleading for Cosette. M. Madeleine, who has slipped in unnoticed, orders her released; she spits in his face. Over Javert's furious protest the mayor invokes the law, dismisses him from the room, and promises Fantine her debts paid, her child brought, and a new life. She kisses his hand and faints.
details: Javert drags Fantine to the police station, sits down and writes in silence while she crouches in a corner like a frightened dog. In his mind he has just witnessed a crime: a creature outside society attacking a citizen and elector. He hands the sergeant his paper and tells Fantine she will have six months. She drags herself across the floor on her knees, begging: six months at seven sous a day, and she owes the Thénardiers over a hundred francs; Cosette will be turned into the street; the gentleman put snow down her back; she was not bad at bottom, she drank brandy only out of misery. Javert tells her the Eternal Father himself could do nothing more, and turns his back.

A man who entered unnoticed and stood listening against the door steps forward: "One moment, if you please." Javert recognises M. Madeleine. At the words "Mr. Mayor" Fantine springs up, stares at the man she blames for everything, laughs, and spits in his face. He wipes it away and says: Inspector Javert, set this woman at liberty. Javert is nearly driven mad; for an instant a hideous comparison between what this woman is and what this mayor might be flickers through his mind. Fantine, bewildered, assumes Javert has freed her and pours out her story to him, cursing the mayor who had her dismissed, explaining how the prison contractors' prices forced her onto the streets, laying his hand on her throat to feel the burning there.

As she reaches the door Javert roars at the sergeant to stop her. "I" gave the order, says Madeleine. Javert, pale and shaking, insists she insulted a citizen, M. Bamatabois, a householder and elector, and that this is a matter for the police. Madeleine answers that he inquired in the square and the citizen was at fault, that the insult to himself is his own to forgive, that the highest law is conscience. When Javert still refuses, the mayor cites the articles of the criminal code that make him the judge in municipal police matters and the law against arbitrary detention, and says: Leave the room. Javert takes the blow like a soldier, bows to the ground, and goes.

Fantine watches the two men who held her life in their hands fight over her, and the angel turns out to be the man she abhorred. Her hatred melts. Madeleine tells her gently that he knew nothing of her dismissal, that he believes her, that he will pay her debts and bring her child or send her to it, that she need never work again, and that in God's sight she has never ceased to be virtuous. She can only sob, kneels, kisses his hand, and faints.

title: The Beginning of Repose
summary: Madeleine nurses Fantine in his own infirmary, learns her whole story, and sends the Thénardiers three hundred francs, then three hundred more, to bring Cosette. Thénardier, scenting a milch cow, invents bills and keeps the child. Fantine's chest disease worsens; the doctor says to fetch the child quickly. Javert posts a letter to the Paris prefecture that the town takes for his resignation.
details: Fantine wakes at noon in the infirmary Madeleine keeps in his own house to find him standing by her bed gazing at the crucifix on the wall, praying, he says, to the martyr on high, and adding to himself, for the martyr here below. He has spent the night and morning making inquiries and knows her story in every detail. From that moment he is transfigured in her eyes.

The same night Javert writes a letter and posts it himself to M. Chabouillet, secretary to the prefect of police in Paris. The postmistress and others who recognise his hand assume, after the scene at the station, that he is resigning.

Madeleine writes to the Thénardiers: Fantine owes a hundred and twenty francs; he sends three hundred and tells them to bring Cosette at once to her sick mother. Thénardier tells his wife not to let the child go, since this lark is turning into a milch cow, and replies with a bill for five hundred odd francs, padded with doctors' and apothecaries' charges that were really for Éponine's and Azelma's illnesses. Madeleine sends three hundred more. Thénardier still does not let go, pleading winter and small debts.

The sisters, at first repelled by "that woman", are won over by her humility; she tells them that having Cosette beside her will be the sign that God has pardoned her. Madeleine visits twice a day and each time promises the child tomorrow, perhaps. But Fantine does not recover: the snow on her bare back has unleashed a chest disease smouldering for years. The doctor sounds her chest, shakes his head, and tells Madeleine to make haste and bring the child. Madeleine shudders, and tells Fantine the doctor says Cosette's arrival will cure her. He declares he will send for Cosette, or go himself, and has Fantine sign a dictated note ordering Thénardier to hand the child to the bearer. Then, the narrator says, a serious incident occurs.

title: How Jean May Become Champ
summary: Javert comes to ask the mayor to have him dismissed: in his rage six weeks ago he denounced M. Madeleine to Paris as the ex-convict Jean Valjean, and he was wrong, because the real Jean Valjean has been found. An old apple-thief called Champmathieu, arrested near Arras, has been recognised as Valjean by three former convicts and by Javert himself, and goes before the Assizes tomorrow. Madeleine refuses to dismiss him; Javert refuses his hand.
details: Madeleine is in his study preparing for a possible trip to Montfermeil when Javert, who has avoided him since the station scene, asks to see him. The mayor keeps his back turned and goes on annotating a docket. Javert, visibly changed, stands in humble, rigid resignation, and announces that an inferior agent has gravely failed in respect towards a magistrate: he himself, towards the mayor. He asks to be turned out, not allowed to resign, since resignation is honourable and he deserves punishment. Six weeks ago, furious over the woman, he informed against the mayor at the prefecture in Paris, as an ex-convict.

The mayor turns livid as Javert explains: a resemblance, inquiries the mayor had made at Faverolles, his strength, the Fauchelevent affair, his marksmanship, a slight drag in his leg, all absurdities, but he had taken him for a certain Jean Valjean, a convict he knew twenty years ago as a guard at Toulon, who after his release robbed a bishop and then a little Savoyard on the highway and vanished eight years ago. Paris replied that Javert was mad, and they were right, because the real Jean Valjean has been found. The paper drops from Madeleine's hand.

Javert tells the story. A wretched old man called Father Champmathieu was arrested last autumn near Ailly-le-Haut-Clocher with a broken branch of stolen apples in his hand. Transferred to the prison at Arras, he was hailed by an ex-convict turnkey, Brevet: you are Jean Valjean, we were at Toulon together. Inquiry found that Champmathieu had been a tree-pruner at Faverolles thirty years before, like Valjean; that Valjean's mother was named Mathieu; that Jean Mathieu, pronounced in Auvergne, becomes Chan Mathieu, then Champmathieu. Two lifers from Toulon, Cochepaille and Chenildieu, were brought to confront him and recognised him. Javert was summoned and recognised him too: the truth is the truth, that man is Jean Valjean. For a convict, climbing a wall and stealing apples is a second offence: the galleys for life. The man only repeats, stupidly, that he is Champmathieu, which Javert takes for cunning. The case is tried at Arras tomorrow; Javert leaves by coach tonight to testify and returns as soon as his deposition is taken.

Madeleine, outwardly indifferent, gives Javert a list of petty police errands, then rises and says he esteems him, that the offence concerns himself alone, and that Javert deserves promotion and shall keep his post. Javert refuses: he has been severe with others all his life and would be a blackguard not to be severe with himself; the kindness that upholds a street-walker against a citizen and a police agent against a mayor is false kindness that disorganises society. He demands the discharge of Inspector Javert. When the mayor offers his hand, Javert recoils: a mayor does not give his hand to a police spy. He will serve until replaced. Madeleine sits listening to the firm steps die away.

title: Sister Simplice
summary: Hugo introduces the two nursing sisters, rough Sister Perpétue and Sister Simplice, who has never in her life told a lie. Madeleine speaks to Simplice about Fantine in a singular tone, stays an hour with the sick woman, hears from the doctor that she is losing ground fast, and is then seen studying a road map of France and pencilling figures.
details: Book VII begins with a warning that not all of what follows was known at Montreuil-sur-Mer, and that two or three improbable details are kept out of respect for the truth. The afternoon after Javert's visit, Madeleine sends for Sister Simplice before going in to Fantine. The two infirmary nuns are Sister Perpétue, a robust peasant who became a nun as another woman becomes a cook, rough with her patients and crabbed with the dying, and Sister Simplice, pale as wax, ageless, gentle, austere and more solid than granite.

Simplice's distinctive trait is that she has never lied, not even the small innocent lie everyone allows himself; to her, Satan has two names, Satan and Lying. She chose her name after Simplice of Sicily, who let her breasts be torn off rather than misstate her birthplace. Her two early faults, a taste for sweets and for letters, she has corrected. She has grown fond of Fantine and devotes herself to her.

Madeleine takes Simplice aside and commends Fantine to her in a singular tone she recalls afterwards. With Fantine, who says she only lives when he is there, he is as usual, answering "Soon" when she asks for Cosette, but stays an hour instead of half an hour. His face darkens when the doctor murmurs that she is losing ground fast. Back at the town hall, the clerk sees him examining a road map of France and writing figures on a scrap of paper.

title: The Perspicacity of Master Scaufflaire
summary: Madeleine hesitates at the priest's door, then hires from the Fleming Scaufflaire a small white horse and a light tilbury to travel twenty leagues, leaving a five-hundred-franc guarantee and refusing to say where he is going. From the figures 5, 6, 8½ left behind, Scaufflaire works out the relays: Hesdin, Saint-Pol, Arras. That night Madeleine's lodger hears him pacing overhead for hours with his window open.
details: On his way to the horse-hirer Madeleine passes the parsonage, stops, turns back, lifts the knocker, holds it, and sets it down gently without knocking before hurrying on. Master Scaufflaire, a Fleming who lets horses and gigs, is asked for a horse that can do twenty leagues in a day hitched to a cabriolet and set out again the next morning. Madeleine shows him a paper with the figures 5, 6 and 8½, nineteen and a half leagues in all.

Scaufflaire offers his little white Boulonnais horse, which will not be ridden but goes like the wind in harness, and sets his terms: a half-hour rest midway with someone watching that the stable boys do not steal the oats, the mayor travelling alone and driving himself, thirty francs a day, and a light open tilbury instead of a cabriolet. Asked whether he has considered the winter cold and the rain, Madeleine says only that horse and tilbury must be at his door at half-past four tomorrow morning. He goes out, comes back, and leaves a five-hundred-franc note as guarantee for a horse and gig worth a hundred crowns, still refusing to say where he is going.
The Fleming and his wife puzzle over it; she guesses Paris. Then he finds the forgotten paper on the mantel: five leagues to Hesdin, six to Saint-Pol, eight and a half to Arras. He is going to Arras.

Madeleine takes the long way home to avoid the parsonage door and shuts himself in his room at half-past eight. The cashier who lodges beneath him wakes at midnight to footsteps pacing overhead, a cupboard opening and closing, furniture moved, and the red flicker of a fire reflected on the opposite wall through a window flung wide in the bitter cold. An hour or two later the step is still pacing. This, says the narrator, is what had taken place in that room.

title: A Tempest in a Skull
summary: The narrator confirms what the reader has guessed: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean. Through a night of torment he argues both ways, to let Champmathieu go to the galleys in his place and go on doing good for a whole town and for Fantine and Cosette, or to denounce himself and save his soul. He burns his old convict's clothes and the forty-sou piece, nearly melts the Bishop's candlesticks, hears a voice cry his name, and ends the night no nearer a decision.
details: Hugo opens by saying the reader has no doubt divined that M. Madeleine is none other than Jean Valjean, and asks us to enter his conscience as Dante entered his door. After the theft from Little Gervais, Valjean sold the Bishop's silver except the candlesticks, crossed France, built his fortune at Montreuil-sur-Mer, and has since lived by two rules that nearly always agree: to hide his name and to sanctify his life. Where they clashed he sacrificed safety to goodness, keeping the candlesticks, mourning the Bishop, questioning the Savoyards, inquiring at Faverolles, lifting Fauchelevent's cart under Javert's eye.

At Javert's first words his instinct was to run and denounce himself; he stifled it, got through the day, visited Fantine, hired the tilbury so as to be ready for anything, dined with appetite, and then bolted his door and put out his light as if his conscience could be shut out. Slowly he sees that he is master of the situation: the name he dreaded has surfaced and, far from menacing him, has made him safer than ever. Javert has his Jean Valjean. Providence has arranged it; who is he to disarrange it? He relights his candle and declares the matter settled, and feels no joy.

The tide of thought returns. To let an innocent man take his place is hypocritical baseness, a theft of another man's life, a moral murder; the Bishop, more present dead than alive, would find Mayor Madeleine abominable and the convict Jean Valjean admirable. He must go to Arras, free the false Valjean and denounce the real one. He puts his books in order, burns bills owed him by poor tradesmen, writes a letter to the banker Laffitte, pockets his passport. He weighs the chances of mercy and remembers that the forty sous from Little Gervais make him a repeat offender liable to the galleys for life. Then he thinks of Fantine and a new crisis opens: if he vanishes, the factory, the town, the mother and the child all perish, for the sake of an old apple-thief who may deserve the galleys anyway. The true self-sacrifice, he decides, is to bear the reproach of his conscience for others' good. "I am Madeleine, and Madeleine I remain."

To cut the last threads, he opens a hidden cupboard in the wall and throws into the fire the blue blouse, trousers, knapsack and iron-shod thorn cudgel he wore into Digne in 1815; among the ashes glints the forty-sou piece. He seizes the two silver candlesticks to melt them too, and a voice within him shouts "Jean Valjean!", telling him to finish, to forget the Bishop, to let an innocent old man wear his red blouse and drag his chain while the whole town blesses him and one voice curses him in the dark, and that only the curse will reach God. He asks aloud if anyone is there, laughs at himself, and sets the candlesticks back on the mantel. He paces on, recoiling from both resolutions in turn, imagining the galleys at his age, the green cap, the chain, the strangers told "that is the famous Jean Valjean who was mayor". Remain in paradise and become a demon, or return to hell and become an angel? The chapter ends with him no further forward than when he began, likened to another man who once pushed away a cup in a garden of olive trees.

title: Forms Assumed by Suffering During Sleep
summary: At three in the morning Jean Valjean drops into his chair and dreams of walking with his long-forgotten brother across a colourless plain into a deserted town where silent earth-coloured men stand behind every door and tell him he has been dead a long time. He wakes to the sound of hooves: Scaufflaire's tilbury is at the door, and the portress announces that it is five o'clock.
details: After five hours of pacing he falls asleep in his chair and has a dream he later wrote down, which Hugo reproduces from the paper in his hand. He walks on a vast grassless plain, neither day nor night, with the brother of his childhood whom he never thinks of, talking of a neighbour who always worked with her window open. A hairless rider the colour of ashes passes on an earth-coloured horse without a word. His brother leads him into a hollow road and vanishes. He enters a village he thinks is Romainville, where every street, house and garden is empty, yet behind each corner, door and tree a man stands silent against the wall and does not answer when asked where he is. Leaving, he turns and finds the whole crowd of these earthen-faced men silently overtaking him. The first one says: do you not know that you have been dead this long time? He opens his mouth to answer and there is no one there.

He wakes icy cold; the fire is out, the candle almost gone, the window still open, no stars in the sky. A harsh sound from below draws his eye to two red lights in the yard, which he first takes for stars fallen to earth, then recognises as the lanterns of a tilbury harnessed to a small white horse. A tap at his door: the old portress, saying it is five o'clock and the cabriolet is here. He denies having ordered any tilbury, until she says M. Scaufflaire's name, which goes through him like lightning. After a long silence he tells her to say it is well, and that he is coming down.

title: Hindrances
summary: Driving at random towards Arras, Jean Valjean collides with the night mail and finds at Hesdin that his wheel is wrecked beyond repair that day. Joyful that Providence has stopped him, he is caught again when a boy fetches an old woman with a ramshackle cart to hire. Over bad roads, a detour, a broken whiffletree and a hired second horse he presses on, realising only at seven in the evening that he never asked when the trial begins.
details: Entering Montreuil-sur-Mer before five, the Arras mail-wagon clips the wheel of a tilbury going the other way at a gallop with a single cloaked man in it, who does not stop. He is going to Arras without having decided anything, telling himself there is no harm in seeing with his own eyes, that no one will recognise him, that he holds his destiny in his hand; at bottom he would rather not go, and the nearer he gets the more something in him draws back. The little Boulonnais horse covers five leagues in two hours.

At the inn at Hesdin the stableman points out that the wheel has two split spokes and a strained hub and will not go another quarter league. The wheelwright Bourgaillard can mend it only by tomorrow; he has no spare wheels, no cabriolet to let or sell, only an old calash needing two post-horses, which on these crossroads at ploughing time would mean waiting hours at every relay; the white horse will not take a saddle; no horse for Arras can be bought or hired for any money; the next mail passes at night. Valjean feels an immense joy. It is Providence that broke the wheel; he has honestly exhausted every means and can turn back with nothing to reproach himself for. He breathes freely for the first time since Javert's visit.

But the conversation took place in the street, and a boy who was listening runs off and returns with an old woman who has a cart to hire: a leaky, rusted basket-cart hanging on leather thongs, but it runs on two wheels and can reach Arras. The iron hand has seized him again. He pays, leaves the tilbury for repair, harnesses the white horse and goes on, angry at the joy he felt a moment before. He refuses the boy who asks a tip for finding the cart.

The heavy cart takes four hours for the five leagues to Saint-Pol, where he watches the horse eat as promised, orders breakfast, and cannot swallow the bread, which tastes bitter. Beyond Tinques a road-mender tells him the main road is barred for repairs; the detour by Carency and Mont-Saint-Éloy adds leagues of crossroads in the dark. He takes the advice to hire a second horse and a stable-boy as postilion at Tinques. The whiffletree breaks in a rut and he cuts a branch to replace it. Starving, frozen, he remembers his other night journey on the plain near Digne eight years before. At seven, with three leagues to go, it occurs to him for the first time that he does not even know the hour of the trial, that Assizes sit at nine and such a case is short, and that he will probably arrive when all is over.

title: Sister Simplice Put to the Proof
summary: Fantine, delirious and sinking, waits all afternoon for the mayor's three o'clock visit that does not come and sings an old cradle song she once sang to Cosette. Learning he has left town, Sister Simplice refuses the maid's suggested lie and says simply that the mayor has gone away. Fantine concludes he has gone to Montfermeil for Cosette and is so overjoyed that the doctor finds her better.
details: The same day, back at the infirmary, Fantine has had a frightful night and is delirious by morning; the doctor asks to be told as soon as M. Madeleine arrives. At twenty-five she has the face of an old woman. She asks Sister Simplice the time again and again as three o'clock, the mayor's punctual hour, approaches, sits up at the stroke and stares at the door for a quarter of an hour, then falls back. The hours pass; she blames no one, only coughs and says low that he is wrong not to come today, since she is going away tomorrow. Then she sings, in a voice like a breath, an old lullaby about buying linen for a child and the Virgin at her stove, which she had sung to Cosette and not remembered in five years. The nun weeps.

At six Sister Simplice sends a maid to the factory portress, who reports that the mayor left before six that morning alone in a tilbury with a white horse, that some say he took the Arras road and others the Paris road, and that he said not to expect him tonight. Fantine, overhearing the whispering, rears up on her knees and demands in a hoarse voice to know why he cannot come. The maid whispers to the nun to say he is busy with the town council. Simplice blushes at the proposed lie, weighs the blow the truth may deal, and then says calmly: Monsieur le Maire has gone away.

Fantine's face blazes with joy: he has gone to fetch Cosette. She prays, apologises for shouting, lies down obediently, kisses the little silver cross Simplice gave her, and talks on in a flood: he need not even go through Paris, Montfermeil is a little to the left; he made her sign the letter; Cosette is seven now and must be a big girl; tomorrow will be a festival and she must wear her lace cap. The sister, who has no idea of distances, agrees that he will be back tomorrow.

Between seven and eight the doctor finds her wide-eyed and asking whether the child may sleep in a little bed beside her, there is just room. Simplice explains their silence and the patient's guess, which may after all be right; he approves. He finds her pulse stronger and the pressure on her chest eased, prescribes quinine and a calming draught, and tells the sister that if the mayor really arrived tomorrow with the child, great joy has been known to arrest even an advanced organic disease; they may yet save her.

title: The Traveller on His Arrival Takes Precautions for Departure
summary: Reaching Arras near eight at night after fourteen hours on the road, Jean Valjean books a seat on the one o'clock mail back to Montreuil-sur-Mer, then finds the Assizes still sitting late in the old bishop's palace. He learns the convict's case is not over, that the hall is full and the door closed, and after hesitating on the stairs sends the President a note: M. Madeleine, Mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer.
details: The cart rolls into the Hotel de la Poste at Arras about eight. Valjean stables the white horse himself, refuses bed and supper, and, told the horse needs two days' rest, goes to the posting office, shows his passport, and buys the vacant seat beside the postboy on the mail-wagon leaving for Montreuil-sur-Mer at one in the morning. Then he wanders the dark unfamiliar streets, loses himself beyond the little river Crinchon, and at last asks an old townsman with a lantern the way to the courthouse. The courts, the man explains, are sitting in the prefecture, the former bishop's palace. Four windows blazing late in the grand square mean the Assizes have not finished; the man wonders if he is a witness. He says he only wants to speak to a lawyer.

In the dim great hall of the old palace, thick with murmuring black-gowned groups, he asks a lawyer what stage they have reached. It is finished, judgment given, for life. His voice falters: so the identity was established? The lawyer is puzzled: there was no identity in question; a woman named Limosin was condemned for killing her child. The lights are for a second case begun two hours ago, a convict up for a second offence, a bandit's face if ever there was one. Valjean has felt, within moments, ice and fire. He listens at the groups: the apple theft is not well proved, but the man was certainly once at Toulon; witnesses are done, speeches remain; the man will be condemned, the prosecutor never misses.

The usher tells him the door will not reopen because the hall is full; there are two or three seats behind the President, but only for public functionaries. He goes slowly down the stairs, leans on the balusters with folded arms, and after a long inner debate tears a leaf from his pocketbook and writes by the street lantern: M. Madeleine, Mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer. He climbs back through the crowd, hands it to the usher, and orders him to take it to the President.

title: An Entrance by Favor
summary: The mayor's name is revered far beyond his district, and the President at once admits him. Left alone in the council-chamber, with only a brass door-handle between him and the courtroom, Jean Valjean stares at an old framed letter without reading it, thinks of Fantine and Cosette, flees down the corridor, stands a quarter of an hour in the dark, comes back, and finds himself through the door.
details: Without knowing it, the mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer is famous across the Bas Boulonnais and the neighbouring departments for his virtue and for the industries he has rescued or financed. The Councillor from Douai presiding over the Arras Assizes knows the name like everyone else, writes a deferential line at the foot of the paper, and says "Admit him." The same usher who turned his back now bows to the ground and hands back the note: the President of the Court of Assizes presents his respects to M. Madeleine. He crushes it as though the words left a bitter taste.

He is led through narrow corridors and dark stairs to the wainscoted council-chamber, two candles on a green cloth, and told that the copper handle of the door opposite opens into the courtroom behind the President's chair. Alone, he cannot gather his thoughts. He has not eaten in twenty-four hours and does not feel it. He stands before a framed autograph letter of Pache, mayor of Paris in the year II, and reads it two or three times without taking in a word, thinking of Fantine and Cosette.

His gaze falls on the brass knob and fills slowly with terror; sweat runs down his temples. With a gesture that says who compels me to this, he turns, goes out by the door he came in, and flees along the lantern-lit corridor as if pursued until he staggers against the cold stone wall. For a quarter of an hour he stands there in the dark, hearing within him only the single word Alas. Then, as though someone had overtaken him and were leading him back, he returns to the council-chamber. The knob shines at him like a terrible star; he cannot look away; step by step he nears it, grasps it without knowing how, and the door opens. He is in the courtroom.

title: A Place Where Convictions Are in Process of Formation
summary: Hidden behind a pile of boxes on the judges' bench, Jean Valjean sees the accused: an old man in a blouse who looks like himself as he was entering Digne, whom everyone calls Jean Valjean. Bamatabois sits on the jury. The defence has argued that the apple theft is unproved and only the identity is attested; the prosecutor has made the lawyer's concessions his own and asked for the galleys for life.
details: He stands inside the door of a vast, ill-lit, smoky hall and sees, on a bench between two gendarmes, a man of about sixty with bristling hair, a wild uneasy eye and a blouse: himself grown old, as he was the day he entered Digne full of hatred. "Shall I become like that again?" The President and the prosecutor, who knows him from Montreuil-sur-Mer, bow to him; he barely notices. Judges, gendarmes and gaping heads are the scene of his own trial twenty-seven years ago come to life, except that a crucifix now hangs above the President, which the courts lacked when he was condemned. Everyone in the room is calling the man in the blouse Jean Valjean. He sinks into a chair and hides his face behind a pile of cardboard boxes on the judges' desk. M. Bamatabois is one of the jurors. He looks for Javert and cannot see him.

The defence has just finished. For three hours the crowd has watched this wretched, stupid or cunning man bend under a terrible likeness. The accusation holds that he is not only a fruit-stealer but the ex-convict Jean Valjean, wanted for the highway robbery of the Savoyard Little Gervais eight years ago, to be tried for that later once his identity is fixed; and that for a convict a new theft is a second offence. The man's whole person is a denial, but he speaks with difficulty and stares at the ceiling. If his identity were established and the Little Gervais affair ended in conviction, even death would be possible.

Counsel for the defence, in the pompous dialect of the provincial bar, argued that no one saw his client scale the wall or break the branch, which he said he found on the ground; that the only proof of the theft is his supposed character as a convict; that four witnesses do recognise him as Jean Valjean and the Faverolles and Jean-Mathieu details are awkward, but even granting that, being Valjean does not prove he stole the apples; that his client's obstinate denial of everything was a bad system which his lawyer advised against, but a brutalised and stupid man should not be condemned for defending himself badly. He asked, at most, the penalty for breaking ban, not the galleys for a second offence.

The district-attorney seized on the defence's "loyalty": the lawyer had as good as admitted the man was Jean Valjean. He blamed the crime on the immoral new romantic literature, painted Valjean as a monster, and listed the four witnesses: Javert, the upright inspector, and the convicts Brevet, Chenildieu and Cochepaille. The accused listened open-mouthed, admiring that a man could talk like that, shaking his head slowly and muttering that this came of not asking M. Baloup. The prosecutor called that stupidity deliberate craft and demanded the full penalty, at that time the galleys for life. The defence rose to reply and visibly lost ground.

title: The System of Denials
summary: Asked if he has anything to add, Champmathieu pours out a rambling account of his life as a wheelwright for M. Baloup in Paris and his dead laundress daughter, and the court laughs. Javert's deposition is read in his absence; Brevet, Chenildieu and Cochepaille are recalled and each swears again that this is Jean Valjean, while the prisoner cries "Famous!". Then a voice behind the judges calls the three convicts by name, and twenty people cry out: M. Madeleine!
details: The President asks the accused whether he has anything to add. The man, twisting a dreadful cap in his hands, does not understand at first, then erupts: he was a wheelwright in Paris with Monsieur Baloup, a hard open-air trade that makes a man old at forty and he was fifty-three; his daughter was a laundress, up to her waist in cold water, later at the steaming Enfants-Rouges wash-house that ruined her eyes; her husband beat her; she is dead; they were not happy; ask M. Baloup. He pauses to salute someone in the crowd. The audience laughs, and not knowing why, he laughs too.

The President explains that Baloup has been summoned in vain, being bankrupt and untraceable, and solemnly asks the prisoner two questions: did he climb the Pierron orchard wall and steal the apples, and is he the discharged convict Jean Valjean, yes or no? The man says "In the first place", stares at his cap and the ceiling, and falls silent. The prosecutor declares his embarrassment condemns him. Stung, the prisoner bursts out again: he is a poor man who does not eat every day, he picked up a broken branch lying on the road after a shower, he has been dragged about for three months, he never heard of Jean Valjean or Jean Mathieu, he does not know where he was born, his parents walked the roads, yes he has been in Auvergne and at Faverolles but can a man not have been there without having been in the galleys? Why is everyone hunting him?

The prosecutor asks to recall the four witnesses. The President notes that Inspector Javert left for his duties as soon as he had testified, so the prosecutor reads his deposition: he needs no circumstantial proof, he recognises the man perfectly as the vicious ex-convict Jean Valjean, nineteen years for theft, five or six escape attempts, suspected also of a theft at the late Bishop of Digne's, whom he often saw as adjutant of the guard at Toulon. Then Brevet is brought in, a sixty-year-old with a businessman's face and a rascal's air, reminded that he cannot swear an oath, and begged to reflect; he insists this is Jean Valjean, who entered Toulon in 1796 and left in 1815, sly then if brutish now. Chenildieu, a small wiry lifer in red cassock and green cap nicknamed I-deny-God, laughs: they were chained together five years. Cochepaille, a half-savage Pyrenean shepherd turned brigand, says he is Jean Valjean, called Jean-the-Screw for his strength.

After each the prisoner mutters, with growing satisfaction, "he's a nice one", "Good!", "Famous!", and when asked what he has to say, repeats "Famous!". Uproar; the man is clearly lost. As the President calls for silence to sum up, a lamentable, terrible voice beside him cries: Brevet! Chenildieu! Cochepaille! look here! A man among the privileged spectators behind the court has risen, pushed through the half-door and stands in the middle of the hall. The President, the prosecutor, Bamatabois and twenty others exclaim together: M. Madeleine!

title: Champmathieu More and More Astonished
summary: His hair turned white in an hour, the man they know as Madeleine tells the court to release the prisoner and arrest him: he is Jean Valjean. When the prosecutor calls for a doctor, he proves it by reminding Brevet of his checked suspenders, Chenildieu of the burn hiding the letters on his shoulder, and Cochepaille of the date tattooed on his arm. No one stops him as he walks out; within the hour the jury frees Champmathieu, who understands nothing.
details: It is he. His coat is buttoned, his hat in his hand, he is very pale, and his hair, grey when he arrived in Arras, has turned entirely white in the hour he sat there. Before anyone can move he walks to the three witnesses and asks if they recognise him; they shake their heads, and Cochepaille, intimidated, salutes. He turns to the jury and court and says gently: order the prisoner released, have me arrested; he is not the man you seek, it is I, I am Jean Valjean.

In the grave-like silence the President exchanges signs with the prosecutor and asks whether a physician is present; the prosecutor, invoking the honourable mayor's reputation, asks that he be attended and taken home. Valjean cuts him off: he is not mad; they were about to commit a great error; he has hidden under another name, grown rich, become mayor and tried to re-enter the ranks of the honest, and it seems that cannot be done. He robbed the Bishop; he robbed Little Gervais; Jean Valjean was a vicious wretch, though perhaps not wholly by his own fault, for the galleys make the convict: he went in a stupid peasant and came out a firebrand, and later kindness saved him as severity had ruined him. The forty-sou piece he stole from Little Gervais seven years ago lies among the ashes of his fireplace. He wishes Javert were here to recognise him.

Since the convicts do not know him, he knows them. Brevet, do you remember the knitted checked suspenders you wore in the galleys? Chenildieu, your right shoulder bears a deep burn where you tried to efface the letters T. F. P., which still show: is it true? "It is true." Cochepaille, near the bend of your left arm is tattooed in blue the date of the Emperor's landing at Cannes, March 1, 1815: pull up your sleeve. A gendarme holds a light to the bare arm, and the date is there. With a smile both of triumph and of despair he says: you see plainly that I am Jean Valjean.

There are no longer judges or prosecutors in the room, only staring eyes and moved hearts; everyone understands at once the history of a man giving himself up so another will not be condemned in his place. No one puts a question or intervenes. He says he will withdraw since they do not arrest him, that he has much to do, and that the district-attorney knows who he is and where he is going and can have him taken when he likes. The crowd parts; the door is found open; at the threshold he tells the prosecutor he is at his command and asks the audience to consider him worthy of pity, though when he thinks of what he nearly did he counts himself to be envied. Less than an hour later the jury acquits Champmathieu, who goes off stupefied, thinking all men fools.
